title: Understand batteries and watt-hours
summary: Watt-hours describe stored energy; watts describe how quickly equipment uses it. Keeping these separate prevents an optimistic battery estimate from becoming an emergency plan.
when: Before buying backup power or deciding which devices to run during an outage.
needs: Device wattage or measured power draw
steps: Write down the battery’s stated watt-hour capacity and its maximum continuous output in watts. A large energy capacity does not imply a high-power outlet.
List each essential device’s running watts and hours of use. Multiply watts by hours to estimate watt-hours; add the devices together.
If only amp-hours are listed, use the battery’s specified nominal voltage: watt-hours = amp-hours × volts. Do not compare milliamp-hour labels at different voltages directly.
Allow for conversion losses, age, cold conditions and reserve power. Check motor startup surge separately and test the actual combination before relying on it.
warnings: A small USB power bank cannot power a household heater or refrigerator unless the whole system is specifically rated for that load. Life-support equipment needs a clinician-approved backup plan.
mistakes: Treating a theoretical runtime as a guarantee.
Forgetting inverter standby consumption or device cycling.
alternatives: Prioritize phone, radio and lighting; relocate for essential equipment that lacks a tested supply.
quick: Energy: Wh. Power: W.
Approximate runtime = usable Wh ÷ device W.

sources.title: Estimating Appliance and Home Electronic Energy Use

title: Charge phones and batteries safely
summary: A working charging plan keeps communications available without introducing a battery fire. Familiar cables and a practiced routine are more useful than a drawer of untested adapters.
when: While preparing backup batteries or sharing limited charging capacity during an outage.
steps: Inspect the battery and cables. Stop using equipment with swelling, leaking, unusual heat, odor, discoloration or odd noises; move away and call emergency services if it smokes or burns.
Use the charger and charging method specified by the manufacturer. Keep devices clear of bedding, paper and other combustible materials and do not cover them.
Give priority to emergency phones and medical communications. Reduce screen use and charge a spare bank while safe power remains available.
Keep batteries dry and within their documented temperature limits. Check charge indicators periodically and schedule recharging before they are needed.
warnings: Do not repair, puncture or improvise connections to lithium battery packs. Never run a vehicle in a garage to charge devices, even with the door open.
mistakes: Charging a damaged battery.
Leaving power banks in a hot car or direct sun.
alternatives: Use a verified community charging location when accessible, taking your own compatible cable and keeping the phone with you.
quick: Inspect first; use the correct charger.
Heat, swelling or smoke means stop.

sources.title: What to Do to Protect Yourself During a Power Outage

title: Plan realistic portable solar charging
summary: Portable solar can replenish a compatible battery in daylight, but panel ratings are not dependable all-day output. Shade and winter weather can sharply limit harvest.
when: When adding an optional charging source to a battery-based outage plan.
needs: Panel and charge controller compatible with the battery
steps: Check panel voltage, connectors and the battery’s accepted solar input. Use the approved controller and cables; similar-looking plugs do not prove electrical compatibility.
Place a portable panel where permitted, with good sunlight and minimal shade, using the maker’s secure mounting guidance. Keep the battery within its temperature and weather limits.
Test a normal day of charging and record energy received if the device reports watt-hours. Repeat in less favorable weather before using the result for planning.
Budget for cloudy days and short winter daylight. Retain a charged reserve and another way to obtain essential power or relocate.
warnings: Do not climb a roof, improvise mains wiring or connect panels directly to household circuits. Rooftop work and building electrical connections need qualified installers.
mistakes: Multiplying rated panel watts by every daylight hour.
Leaving a non-weatherproof battery in rain.
alternatives: A smaller device load, spare charged banks or a community charging site may be more reliable than a shaded balcony panel.
quick: Match the equipment.
Measure actual harvest; keep a reserve.

title: Light a home without mains power
summary: Battery lighting makes stairs, food preparation and nighttime movement easier without the fire risk of candles. Arrange lighting before darkness rather than searching room by room.
when: When power fails or preparing a kit for each household member.
needs: LED flashlight or headlamp per person
steps: Place a light at the bed, main exit and route to the bathroom. Keep exits and stairs clear, and use a headlamp for tasks needing both hands.
Choose the lowest useful brightness. Turn off unused lights and reserve one reliable light for emergencies rather than running every lamp continuously.
Keep spare batteries organized by type, with terminals protected from loose metal. Follow the light’s battery and charging instructions.
Test lights during routine supply checks. Replace leaking batteries and keep lights where a guest or caregiver can find them in the dark.
warnings: Use flashlights instead of candles during outages. Never use a fuel lantern or camping stove indoors as a light or heat source.
mistakes: Using a phone flashlight until the communication battery is exhausted.
Putting lanterns where they can fall down stairs.
alternatives: A battery-operated flameless candle can mark a hallway, but retain a real flashlight for hazards and evacuation.
quick: One accessible light per person.
Keep an emergency reserve.

sources.title: What to Do to Protect Yourself During a Power Outage

title: Operate a portable generator safely
summary: Generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide, an invisible gas that can kill rapidly. Outdoor placement and safe electrical connections come before fuel or runtime calculations.
when: Only when a portable fuel-powered generator can be used outdoors according to its manual.
steps: Place the generator outside at least 20 feet from the home, doors, windows and vents, directing exhaust away. Never use it in a garage, basement, balcony enclosure or partly enclosed space.
Check CO alarms and keep the generator dry using only a manufacturer-permitted setup. Do not touch wet equipment or operate it in unsafe rain or flood conditions.

Connect permitted loads with correctly rated heavy-duty outdoor cords. Check continuous and starting loads against the manual; a household connection requires a qualified electrician and approved transfer equipment.
Turn the engine off and let it cool before refueling. Store fuel as local rules and the manual require, away from living spaces and ignition sources.
warnings: Never plug a generator into a wall outlet: backfeeding can kill utility workers. If a CO alarm sounds or poisoning is suspected, get everyone into fresh air immediately and call 911.
mistakes: Assuming an open garage door makes exhaust safe.
Refueling a running or hot generator.
alternatives: Use battery power for small loads or relocate to a powered location when safe generator placement is impossible.
quick: Outdoors, at least 20 feet away.
No backfeeding. Cool before refueling.

sources.title: Keep Your Family, Pets Safe When Using Generators
What to Do to Protect Yourself During a Power Outage

title: Use extension cords without fire hazards
summary: An extension cord is a temporary connection with a rated limit. Damaged, overloaded or trapped cords can overheat even when a device appears to work.
when: When temporarily powering permitted equipment or arranging a generator connection.
needs: Intact cord rated for the setting and load
steps: Inspect the cord, plug and outlet for damage, heat marks or loose connections. Replace damaged equipment instead of covering a defect with tape.
Match the cord rating to the intended load and choose outdoor-rated equipment outdoors. Keep connections dry and follow the generator or appliance manual.
Route cords where they cannot be pinched by doors, hidden under rugs or damaged by traffic. Keep walking routes clear and protect children from exposed connections.
Avoid overloaded strips, chained power strips and improvised adapters. Ask an electrician for permanent outlets or any uncertain household wiring problem.
warnings: Plug major household appliances directly into suitable wall outlets in normal use. Do not use an extension cord for a space heater. Generator connections must follow generator and appliance instructions.
mistakes: Removing a ground pin.
Treating a cool plug as proof the whole circuit is safe.
alternatives: Move the small device near a proper outlet or use a suitably rated battery-operated alternative.
quick: Inspect, rate, keep dry.
No rugs, pinching or daisy chains.

sources.title: Keep Your Family, Pets Safe When Using Generators

title: Stay warm during a winter outage
summary: Warm clothing, a smaller occupied room and an early relocation plan reduce cold exposure. A home can become unsafe before someone realizes how cold they are.
when: When normal heating stops during cold weather.
needs: Dry layered clothing, hats and blankets
steps: Check for immediate hazards and whether anyone depends on powered medical equipment. Call for help and relocate early if a safe backup is unavailable.
Gather in a suitable room, close curtains and unused room doors, and reduce drafts without blocking required ventilation, alarms or exits.
Wear loose dry layers and use blankets or sleeping bags. Check children, older adults and neighbors frequently for confusion, unusual sleepiness or persistent shivering.
Monitor conditions and official shelter information. Leave for a heated safe location before travel becomes difficult; bring medicines, pets and communication supplies.
warnings: Never heat a home with an oven, outdoor camp stove, grill, charcoal burner or generator. Confusion, severe cold symptoms or a CO alarm require immediate action, fresh air as appropriate and emergency help.
mistakes: Waiting for a specific indoor temperature before considering vulnerable people.
Assuming alcohol makes a person safely warmer.
alternatives: Arrange an accessible stay with a friend or a confirmed warming center; do not assume a shelter is open or accepts all pets.
quick: Layer, reduce drafts, check people.
Relocate before cold becomes an emergency.

sources.title: What to Do to Protect Yourself During a Power Outage

title: Recognize a cold medical emergency
summary: Hypothermia is a dangerous loss of body heat. It can occur indoors or in cool wet conditions, not only in freezing weather.
when: When a cold-exposed person is confused, unusually drowsy, clumsy, slurring speech or shivering heavily.
steps: Call 911 for suspected hypothermia. Do not wait for a thermometer reading or assume a person who stops shivering has recovered.
Move the person gently into a warm shelter if safe. Remove wet clothing and cover with dry layers, including the head and neck while keeping the face clear.
Warm the center of the body first with blankets and gentle body warmth. Handle the person carefully and follow emergency dispatcher instructions.
Stay with them, monitor breathing, and follow dispatcher guidance if breathing is absent or abnormal. Arrange urgent medical care even if they appear to improve.
warnings: Do not rub the person, use intense direct heat or give alcohol. Do not give food or drink to someone who is drowsy, unconscious or unable to swallow normally.
mistakes: Sending a confused person alone to fetch supplies.
Delaying a call while trying repeated home warming methods.
alternatives: If a heated building is not immediately accessible, protect from wind and wet ground while calling for rescue.
quick: Confusion after cold exposure: call 911.
Shelter, dry layers, gentle core warming.

title: Respond to suspected frostbite
summary: Freezing can injure skin and deeper tissue, especially fingers, toes, ears and nose. Numbness is a warning, not a sign that the cold is harmless.
when: When cold-exposed skin becomes numb, unusually pale, waxy or firm.
needs: Loose dry protection for the affected area
steps: Move indoors or out of the wind and address possible hypothermia first. Call emergency services for severe symptoms, confusion or a person who cannot reach shelter.
Remove wet or constricting items gently. Protect the area from pressure and further exposure; seek medical assessment for suspected frostbite.
Use gentle warming, such as body heat, while arranging help. Warm, not hot, water may be appropriate if advised and the area can stay warm afterward.
Avoid walking on frostbitten feet unless necessary to reach safety. Keep damaged areas loosely protected and follow professional instructions.
warnings: Never rub frostbitten tissue or use a fire, heating pad or hot water to thaw numb skin. Do not thaw tissue where it could freeze again; obtain rescue and medical advice.
mistakes: Rubbing fingers with snow.
Returning outside because numbness temporarily improves.
alternatives: Protect the affected part, keep the rest of the person warm and request assistance when safe rewarming cannot be maintained.
quick: Get to shelter and seek medical care.
No rubbing or intense heat.

title: Recognize and respond to heat exhaustion
summary: Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea or clammy skin after heat exposure can signal heat exhaustion. Prompt cooling can prevent worsening illness.
when: During hot indoor conditions, outdoor work or a cooling outage.
needs: Safe drinking water if fully alert
steps: Stop activity and move the person into a cooler place. Loosen unnecessary clothing and have them rest while someone stays nearby.
Cool the body with wet cloths or a cool bath if this can be done safely. Use available help to find an air-conditioned place instead of relying on an overheated room.
Offer small sips of water only if the person is awake, not vomiting and able to swallow normally. Follow any existing clinician-directed fluid restrictions.

Get immediate medical attention for vomiting, worsening symptoms or symptoms lasting longer than one hour. Confusion, fainting or altered behavior may indicate heat stroke: call 911 and begin cooling.
warnings: Heat stroke can occur with sweating. Do not wait for dry skin or a measured high temperature before calling for emergency help.
mistakes: Resuming strenuous work as soon as dizziness fades.
Leaving an ill person alone in a hot room.
alternatives: Contact local officials or a trusted person for transport to a confirmed cooling location; avoid unnecessary heat exposure during travel.
quick: Stop, move to cool shelter, cool skin.
Worsening or confusion: urgent help.

title: Heat stroke: call for emergency help
summary: Confusion, slurred speech, collapse, seizures or loss of consciousness in a hot setting may be heat stroke. This is a life-threatening emergency, even if the person is sweating.
when: Immediately when severe heat illness or altered mental status is suspected.
needs: Shaded or cooled place with safe access
steps: Call 911 immediately. Explain the heat exposure and symptoms, put the phone on speaker if useful and follow dispatcher instructions.
Move the person to a cooler place if you can do so safely. Remove excess outer clothing and begin active cooling without delaying emergency care.
Wet the skin and apply cool wet cloths or use other safe cooling methods directed by the dispatcher. Keep the airway clear and do not leave the person alone.
Monitor breathing until help arrives. If breathing is absent or abnormal, follow dispatcher instructions for CPR and obtain an AED if available.
warnings: Do not give fluids to a person with suspected heat stroke. Do not wait for a thermometer reading, dry skin or improvement before calling 911.
mistakes: Treating confusion as simple tiredness.
Driving an unconscious person alone instead of activating emergency care.
alternatives: If air conditioning is unavailable, use shade and water-based cooling immediately while arranging emergency help.
quick: Call 911; start cooling now.
No drinks; monitor breathing.

title: Set up a NOAA weather radio
summary: A weather-band receiver offers another route to official warnings when mobile data fails. It still depends on a working transmitter, receiver power and adequate reception.
when: Before severe weather or when phone alerts are unreliable.
needs: NOAA Weather Radio receiver with battery backup
Receiver manual and local transmitter information
steps: Check that the radio receives the NOAA weather band. An ordinary AM/FM-only radio cannot receive these broadcasts.
Tune to the strongest relevant local transmitter and follow the manual to enable tone alerts. If available, program SAME county codes for the places you need to monitor.
Install backup batteries and test reception in the room where the radio will stay. Building construction can affect reception; move it if the signal is poor.
Learn how to recognize a test and an actual warning. Review setup when moving, replacing batteries or changing the area you want to monitor.
warnings: Do not assume any hand-crank radio automatically provides nighttime warning alerts. Verify the features and power requirements of your particular model.
mistakes: Leaving alerts disabled after a test.
Relying on outdoor sirens as the only indoor warning system.
alternatives: Use local broadcast radio and enabled phone alerts as additional channels; keep more than one warning method where possible.
quick: Weather band + alert feature + backup power.
Tune and test before the storm.

title: Create a household communication plan
summary: People may be separated when an emergency starts. A shared written plan reduces repeated calls and uncertainty when networks or power are unreliable.
when: During routine preparation, especially for households with children, caregivers or accessibility needs.
needs: Agreement from household and support contacts
steps: Collect phone numbers for household members, caregivers, workplaces and an agreed out-of-area contact. Ask contacts whether they can serve in that role.
Choose nearby and out-of-neighborhood meeting places. Include an accessible route, transport arrangements and how people will check in if they cannot travel.
Share paper copies and store a copy on each phone. Include essential medical and accommodation information only as appropriate for the people carrying it.
Practice a short check-in message and a missed-contact procedure. Review the plan when numbers, schools, health needs or living arrangements change.
warnings: Neither a saved contact nor a messaging app guarantees a working connection. Establish an in-person fallback that does not require everyone to receive a message.
mistakes: Keeping every number on one phone.
Choosing a meeting point that requires crossing a likely hazard.
alternatives: A simple wallet card and two agreed meeting places are a useful start even before a detailed household plan is complete.
quick: Collect, share, practice.
Paper copies and an offline fallback.

sources.title: Create Your Family Emergency Communication Plan

title: Communicate when cellular service is disrupted
summary: Power failures and congestion can interrupt both calls and data. Short messages may be easier to deliver than voice calls, but complete network loss prevents either.
when: When calls fail, mobile data is intermittent or you need to preserve phone power.
steps: For immediate danger, try 911. If the call cannot connect, seek another safe way to get help; text-to-911 availability varies and must be checked in advance.
For nonurgent updates, send a brief text with your location, condition and next planned check-in to the agreed contact. Avoid repeated long calls that consume power and network capacity.
Enable battery saving, reduce unnecessary screen use and stop unneeded background activity. Keep essential alerts enabled when a usable connection exists.
Use the household’s written meeting and check-in plan if communications remain unavailable. Monitor a working local radio for official information.
warnings: SMS, internet messaging, Wi-Fi calling and phone alerts all depend on functioning infrastructure. This app does not transmit emergency messages or create a mesh network.
mistakes: Assuming a sent icon proves a message was received.
Draining the battery repeatedly refreshing a failed connection.
alternatives: A landline, staffed public safety location or trusted neighbor may help if accessible without entering danger.
quick: Emergency: try 911.
Nonurgent: brief text, conserve battery, use the written fallback.

sources.title: Create Your Family Emergency Communication Plan

title: Prepare navigation without mobile data
summary: An address on a phone is not an evacuation route. Paper maps and previously downloaded maps help when coverage fails, while official road closures still take priority.
when: Before travel or evacuation during an infrastructure disruption.
needs: Offline maps downloaded in a separate navigation app if used
steps: Mark home, meeting places, hospitals and confirmed shelter options on a paper map. Include transport arrangements for people who cannot drive or walk far.
If using an offline navigation app, download the relevant area in advance and test it with network access disabled. Save destination addresses separately.
Identify more than one route and avoid relying on a single bridge, low road or public transit connection. Check official instructions before leaving when possible.
Carry maps, phone power, appropriate clothing and essential supplies. Follow barriers and evacuation routes rather than blindly following a stored route.
warnings: Offline maps do not know every new flood, fire, closure or structural hazard. Never enter floodwater or a restricted area because a map shows a road.
mistakes: Assuming all map tiles are cached after viewing them once.
Relying on this app for live mapping or route guidance.
alternatives: Ask local officials for an accessible safe route and keep a printed map with the emergency bag.
quick: Download and test ahead of time.
Carry paper; obey current closures.

title: Use short-range radios responsibly
summary: Two-way radios can connect nearby people without a cellular network when both ends have compatible working equipment. Buildings, terrain, power and channel congestion limit performance.
when: Planning local household or neighborhood coordination in the United States.
steps: Identify the radio service before transmitting. Certified FRS units are generally license-by-rule; GMRS operation normally requires an FCC individual license. Amateur radio has separate licensing rules.
Choose lawful equipment for the intended service and read its manual. Agree on a channel, check-in times and simple plain-language messages with the people who will participate.
Test the actual route between locations, including indoors, and identify where reception fails. Do not treat advertised range as a reliable urban distance.
Keep spare power, listen before speaking and give emergency traffic priority. Verify current FCC rules before purchasing or changing equipment.
warnings: Radio channels are shared and conversations are not private; “privacy codes” do not encrypt them. A consumer radio is not a guaranteed way to reach emergency responders.
mistakes: Assuming all walkie-talkies are license-free.
Expecting an unmanned radio to hear an emergency call.
alternatives: Use a written meeting plan and a designated local contact when the tested radio link cannot cover the area.
quick: Identify the service and licensing.
Agree, test, keep spare power.

sources.title: Create Your Family Emergency Communication Plan

title: Prepare and practice a fire escape
summary: A home fire can leave very little time to escape. Working alarms, clear exits and a practiced meeting place matter more than trying to collect belongings.
when: During household preparation or immediately when smoke or a fire alarm signals danger.
steps: Put smoke alarms in and outside sleeping areas and on every level, following manufacturer and local requirements. Test monthly and maintain or replace alarms as directed.
Identify two usable exits from each room where possible. Keep doors, windows and paths clear; arrange assistance for anyone who needs it.
Practice reaching an outside meeting place. Apartment residents should follow the building’s fire plan and know stair exits and any evacuation assistance arrangements.
If fire occurs, get outside immediately when the escape route is safe, stay outside and call 911. Tell firefighters about anyone missing rather than reentering.
warnings: Do not use elevators in a fire or reenter for possessions or pets. If smoke or heat blocks escape, close a door between you and the fire and call 911 with your exact location.
mistakes: Disabling a smoke alarm because of nuisance alarms.
Blocking an exit with emergency supply boxes.
alternatives: Ask the local fire department about alarm assistance and an accessible escape plan before an emergency.
quick: Alarm, clear exits, outside meeting point.
Get out, stay out, call 911.

title: Take shelter during a tornado warning
summary: A tornado warning means shelter immediately. A sturdy building’s lowest interior area offers better protection than windows, a vehicle or a mobile home.
when: When a tornado warning is issued or a tornado is approaching.
needs: Shoes and head protection if immediately available
steps: Go promptly to a storm shelter, basement or small windowless interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building. Avoid windows and outside walls.
Protect the head and neck with your arms and available sturdy padding. Keep shoes on for debris after the storm and bring essential mobility aids if within reach.
If you live in a mobile home, arrange a nearby sturdy shelter beforehand and move there before dangerous conditions arrive. Follow local instructions.
Continue monitoring official warnings from the sheltered area. Afterward, avoid fallen lines, broken glass and damaged structures until conditions are assessed.
warnings: Do not shelter under a bridge or overpass. Never delay reaching shelter to film the storm or gather supplies. Vehicles and mobile homes are unsafe shelter choices.
mistakes: Opening windows to equalize pressure.
Waiting to see a tornado before responding to a warning.
alternatives: Identify a public sturdy shelter and accessible transport in advance if your home lacks a suitable place.
quick: Warning: shelter now.
Lowest interior room; protect head and neck.

title: Avoid floodwater and electrical hazards
summary: Floodwater can hide current, damaged roads, sewage and live electrical equipment. Avoiding contact is safer than guessing depth or trying to protect possessions.
when: When water rises around roads, the building or utility equipment.
steps: Move to higher ground promptly when flooding threatens and obey evacuation orders. Do not wait until a familiar route is under water.
Never walk or drive through floodwater or around road barriers. Turn around and use an officially safe route; shallow moving water can knock a person down.
Stay out of flooded basements and rooms with submerged outlets, wiring or appliances. Do not enter water to reach a breaker or retrieve belongings.
If trapped, move to the highest safe accessible point and call 911 with your location. After the water recedes, obtain official guidance before entering damaged buildings or using affected utilities.
warnings: Water may be electrically energized or chemically contaminated even if it looks clear. Do not use a generator or electrical equipment in wet conditions.
mistakes: Driving a familiar road because the water looks shallow.
Touching wet appliances after the power seems to be out.
alternatives: Arrange transport and an accessible higher-ground destination before a flood warning when possible.
quick: Higher ground, no floodwater contact.
Never enter water to switch off electricity.

title: Shelter in place for the specific hazard
summary: Sheltering instructions differ for severe weather, hazardous air and other incidents. Follow the local instruction for the actual hazard rather than using one sealed-room routine for everything.
when: When local officials instruct you to remain inside or moving outside would expose you to an immediate hazard.
steps: Read or listen to the complete official instruction: what happened, which area is affected and what actions are requested. Bring people and pets inside when directed.

Choose the room suited to the hazard. Tornado shelter usually means the lowest interior space; an outdoor chemical release may require a different room and ventilation controls specified by officials.
Close doors and windows and change ventilation only as instructed for the incident. Keep essential medicines, water, communication equipment and accessibility aids with you.
Continue monitoring official updates and wait for the all-clear or evacuation direction. Record when instructions were received if multiple reports conflict.
warnings: Do not seal a room containing a combustion appliance or run outdoor fuel equipment indoors. Fire, a gas leak, a CO alarm or rising floodwater can make staying inside unsafe.
mistakes: Treating all shelter instructions as identical.
Opening windows to investigate a hazardous release.
alternatives: If the building itself is unsafe, leave by a safe route and contact emergency services for guidance.
quick: Identify the hazard; follow local instructions.
Use the right room and monitor updates.

sources.title: Recognizing and Responding to Pipeline Emergencies

title: Leave early with an accessible evacuation plan
summary: A planned departure reduces last-minute decisions. Transportation, medicines, mobility needs and pets must be included before an official order makes time short.
when: When evacuation is ordered or your building becomes unsafe.
needs: Emergency bag, medicines and essential documents
steps: Follow evacuation orders immediately using designated routes. If the building has fire, gas or another immediate hazard, leave without delaying for supplies.
When time permits, take medicines, essential equipment, identification, water, phone power and pets. Use a manageable bag and prearranged accessible transportation.
Inform the agreed out-of-area contact where you are going. Confirm a destination or shelter is open and can meet accessibility and pet needs when communication is possible.
Lock up only if safe. Shut utilities off only when instructed or required for a known hazard and you can do so safely; do not delay departure. Wait for authorities before returning.
warnings: Never enter floodwater or pass road barriers. A map or old shelter listing cannot confirm that a route or facility is currently safe.
mistakes: Waiting to pack a full household while danger increases.
Assuming every shelter accommodates every pet or medical device.
alternatives: Arrange multiple destinations and helpers in advance; contact emergency services if trapped or unable to leave safely.
quick: Follow orders; take essentials if safe.
Use safe routes and an agreed contact.

sources.title: Get Moving When a Storm Threatens

title: Locate and label your water shutoff
summary: Knowing the household shutoff can limit damage from a plumbing leak. Find it during normal conditions rather than while water is spreading toward electrical equipment.
when: During preparation or a known household supply leak when access is safe.
needs: Valve location from landlord or plumber
Durable label and emergency plumber contact
steps: Ask the landlord, building manager or plumber which valve controls your home. Apartments may have shared systems; do not operate an unlabeled communal valve.
Locate the household main and individual fixture shutoffs. Label the appropriate valve and record its location in the notebook, including access arrangements.
Have a professional address corrosion, stiffness or an unclear valve. Learn the operation for that exact valve without forcing it or damaging the pipe.
For a leak, turn off the identified supply only if you can reach it safely. Keep people away from wet electrical equipment and call the appropriate plumbing or building professional.
warnings: Never enter standing water to operate a valve near electrical equipment. Do not use a public street valve or force a seized valve without utility or professional direction.
mistakes: Assuming every valve turns the same way.
Closing a shared valve without building approval.
alternatives: A fixture shutoff may isolate a minor leak if clearly identified and safe; otherwise call the building manager or plumber.
quick: Identify, label, record.
Unsafe access: stay clear and call help.

title: Know your electrical panel and its limits
summary: A labeled panel helps an electrician or household member respond to an ordinary problem. It does not make exposed wiring, a wet panel or repeated breaker trips safe to repair.
when: During preparation, or when arranging professional help for an electrical problem.
steps: Find the panel and ask the landlord or electrician to explain the main disconnect and labels. Record the location and keep required access clear.
Inspect only from a safe distance for obvious damage, water, heat, sparks or unusual sounds. Do not remove covers or touch exposed parts.
For sparks, burning odor, floodwater or damaged wiring, leave the area and call emergency services or the utility as appropriate. Do not approach a wet panel.
Have a licensed electrician investigate repeated trips, loose outlets or damaged circuits. Utility restoration and generator connections must use approved equipment and qualified work.
warnings: Never enter standing water to switch off electricity. Never bypass a breaker, fit a larger fuse or backfeed a wall outlet with a generator. A power outage does not prove wires are dead.
mistakes: Repeatedly resetting a breaker without finding the cause.
Using the panel as a storage shelf.
alternatives: Disconnect a small faulty device only when the plug and surroundings are dry and safe; otherwise stay away and request professional assistance.
quick: Know the location; keep access clear.
Wet, sparking or damaged: stay away.

title: Suspected gas leak: leave the area
summary: A rotten-egg smell, hissing or another sign of escaping gas calls for prompt evacuation. Investigating or operating switches can create ignition sparks.
when: Immediately when a gas leak is suspected indoors or near a service line.
needs: Phone used only from a safe distance
Utility emergency contact recorded in advance
steps: Get everyone away from the suspected leak immediately. Do not stop to search for its source or collect belongings.
Avoid flames, smoking, starting engines, switches, garage door openers and phone use in the leak area. Do not turn electrical equipment on or off.
Once well away from the leak, call 911 and the gas utility’s emergency number. Explain the smell or sound and the location; warn others away if this is safe.
Remain outside and wait for professional clearance. Before any future emergency, ask the utility about the particular meter’s shutoff procedure and who should operate it.
warnings: Do not return to repair a pipe or relight appliances. If gas is shut off, only a qualified professional should restore it. Do not practice by actually shutting the gas off.
mistakes: Using a phone beside the suspected leak.
Treating a fading smell as proof the building is safe.
alternatives: If the leak blocks the normal exit, use another safe exit and call for emergency assistance once clear.
quick: Leave first; avoid sparks.
Call from well away; professionals restore service.

sources.title: Recognizing and Responding to Pipeline Emergencies

title: Reduce frozen-pipe risk without unsafe heat
summary: Water expands when it freezes and can break a pipe. Prevention and early plumbing help are safer than improvised flames or risky electrical thawing in a damp area.
when: Before a freeze or when a faucet produces only a trickle during freezing weather.
needs: Pipe insulation suitable for the installation
steps: Before cold weather, protect exposed pipes and disconnect outdoor hoses according to your plumbing arrangement. Ask a plumber about vulnerable pipes and approved insulation.
When heat is operating, open sink cabinet doors to let warmer room air reach pipes, keeping cleaners away from children. Follow local advice about a small drip from vulnerable faucets.
If a pipe appears frozen, keep the affected faucet open and seek a plumber if the frozen section is hidden, inaccessible or uncertain.
If a pipe bursts, use the identified water shutoff only from a safe dry location. Keep away from wet electrical areas and obtain professional repair.
warnings: Never use a blowtorch, propane heater, charcoal stove or other open flame to thaw pipes. Do not use electrical thawing equipment around standing water.
mistakes: Assuming a thawed pipe cannot leak.
Leaving for days without a heat or pipe-protection plan.
alternatives: A plumber can advise safe draining or winterization when heat cannot be maintained.
quick: Insulate early; know the shutoff.
No open flames; call a plumber.

title: Assemble a practical household repair kit
summary: A small organized kit helps contain minor problems and maintain supplies. Tools support safe observation and basic tasks; they do not replace licensed electrical, gas or structural work.
when: When preparing for temporary household disruptions and routine maintenance.
needs: Flashlight, screwdriver, pliers and adjustable wrench
Tape, ties and appropriate small repair supplies
steps: Choose tools for tasks you already know how to perform safely, such as tightening a loose non-electrical fitting or opening a supply container. Include a manual can opener.
Store tools together in a dry accessible place and keep sharp parts and chemicals away from children. Add labels and the locations of household utility controls.
Keep instructions for equipment with the kit and inspect tools for damage. Use each tool for its intended purpose; do not improvise utility keys or repairs.
Write down the building manager, utility and licensed professional contacts. Stop if there are electrical, gas, structural, sewage or major-water hazards.
warnings: Never enter an unsafe area to save property or use a tool you cannot operate safely. Do not mix household chemicals or transfer them to food containers.
mistakes: Buying many specialized tools without learning safe use.
Keeping the only flashlight inside a hard-to-find toolbox.
alternatives: Use a bucket to contain a small clean-water drip only when the surroundings are electrically safe, then arrange a proper repair.
quick: Small, labeled, dry and accessible.
Contain minor problems; call professionals for hazards.
